name: Femi Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. This is confidential. What would a normal working day be like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at a large mine. I check the tyres and brakes before the first run, follow the banksman's signal at the tip, and write faults on a paper sheet for the mechanic. I'm fairly new to this and still ask about ground I don't trust. The truck feels settled when I get the turn right. My partner Lena and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, so cancelled overtime shows up at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the men on the bench that a machine can't read the ground through the seat of my truck. A little software in the office is fine by me if the shift starts on time. I don't see why every new screen needs a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm new enough that I still check where the banksman wants me before I tip. Even with no big AI change, I worry when the mine cancels a Saturday shift. Our mortgage payment comes out whether I get overtime or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep driving the haul truck and writing down anything odd on the paper defect sheet. My partner Lena and I would skip the winter trip we'd been discussing and keep that money for a missed shift. I wouldn't sign up for some new app just to prove I'm modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved about the machines, still tight in the chest about money. I know people hear 'mining pay' and imagine we have a pile of cash, but ours is a few months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a Saturday shift was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I showed Lena the roster at the kitchen table and we put the trip brochure away. Our youngest was annoyed, but I couldn't spend money that might cover a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about keeping a paper defect sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mechanic can see exactly when I heard the rattle, and I don't have to find the right menu with gloves on. I've only been on this truck a short time, so those notes help me ask sensible questions.

say: I'd tell the crew **ground judgement** still matters in a haul truck.
I'd accept office software if it helps the **shift start** on time.
think: I still need the banksman's guidance, and cancelled **overtime** already worries me.
A few months of expenses cannot cover many missed **mortgage payments**.
do: Keep driving the **haul truck** and logging faults on paper.
Skip the planned **winter trip** and hold its cost against a missed shift.
feel: Relieved about limited AI, but **uneasy** about earnings.
S0.quote: Our mortgage payment comes out whether I get overtime or not.
fieldNote: Femi talks about screens with irritation, yet his main pressure in this mild case is **unreliable overtime**.
The postponed **winter trip** is a specific household sacrifice, rather than a reaction to a breakthrough.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck and recording faults on paper
Skip the planned winter trip to cover a missed shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can change its booking and buying systems, but dispatch must still tell us where to go. If they start squeezing more loads into a shift because a computer drew a neat line, I'd want someone to ride the route first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning jobs could go before mine driving does. That still reaches me if a smaller dispatch team makes a mistake or the boss uses software targets to cut overtime. I'm slow with new systems, and I know a younger operator may get picked first for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor for the printed route sheet and keep working my truck. In the first year, if overtime drops, Lena and I would stop paying for the children's weekend lessons for a term. I'd speak at the crew meeting about route checks, even if I dislike making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like the feeling of a timetable coming from a screen I can't question. I'm not in a panic; there are other pits nearby, but they'd have their own targets too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would stopping the lessons be the first cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the winter trip. The children go swimming on Saturdays, and I hate telling them a grown-up budget has decided their time in the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the crew meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a driver to test each new route before it becomes a target. I wouldn't give a speech about AI; I just want a road that the truck can actually take.

say: I'd ask for a driver to **test routes** before new software targets become shift rules.
I'd say office changes must still leave **dispatch** able to answer a driver.
think: AI can shrink **planning staff** first and still push unsafe targets onto my truck.
I may be passed over for **training** because I take longer with unfamiliar screens.
do: Ask the supervisor for a **printed route sheet** and keep driving.
Speak at the **crew meeting** about testing each proposed route.
Pause the children's **weekend swimming lessons** for a term if overtime falls.
feel: **Uneasy** about unchallengeable targets and lost overtime.
S1.quote: I don't like the feeling of a timetable coming from a screen I can't question.
fieldNote: Femi draws a clear line from **office automation** to the driver's routes, despite the low thinking-AI exposure of his own job.
His reluctant **crew meeting** intervention concerns a physical road test, while a fall in overtime reaches the children's lessons.

steps.text: Keep driving with a printed route sheet from the supervisor
Speak at the crew meeting for driver-tested routes
Pause weekend swimming lessons for one term if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2028 could take the office desks, but it won't drive my truck that morning. Then I'd ask what the mine intends to do when capable robots arrive around 2031. Two years is hardly enough to sort the paperwork, never mind the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 when the thinking work changes and 48 when the robot date comes. I don't expect a junior driver like me to be the one they keep. I haven't used AI tools at all, and the thought of starting another trade while the mortgage is due makes me feel sick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking every paid truck shift while they offer it. This month I'd ask Lena to list our fixed bills with me, and we'd cancel the children's swimming lessons before touching mortgage payments. In 2029 I'd apply for driving vacancies at the two nearby pits, though I know robots could reach those seats too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lie awake with this one. The truck is the job I finally got into, and the end of the seat feels close enough to count school terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course if the mine offered one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine paid my wages while I trained for mechanical work, I'd ask about it. I wouldn't quit the truck for an unpaid course, and I'm not pretending mechanics can't face robots later. Right now I need the pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the cancelled lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children I need to protect the mortgage while work changes. I wouldn't blame a robot that hasn't arrived; I'd say we are tightening things until I know what hours I have.

say: I'd ask the mine for a **robot plan** after the 2028 change to office work.
I'd tell colleagues two years gives families little time to **prepare**.
think: By **2031** I may lose the truck seat, and I am too junior to assume a new role.
I have never used AI tools, and an unpaid **career change** feels impossible with the mortgage.
do: Keep taking every paid **truck shift** while the mine offers it.
List fixed **household bills** with Lena and cancel swimming lessons before missing mortgage payments.
Apply to two nearby **driving vacancies** in 2029, knowing robots may later reach them.
feel: **Alarmed** enough to lose sleep over the truck seat.
S2.quote: The truck is the job I finally got into, and the end of the seat feels close enough to count school terms.
fieldNote: Femi expects **office work** to change in 2028 and his own driving to be threatened around 2031.
He considers paid mechanical training only **conditionally**; immediate plans are wages, household cuts, and applications for familiar work.

steps.text: Keep taking paid haul truck shifts while available
Cancel the children’s swimming lessons after listing fixed bills
Apply for two nearby driving vacancies in 2029
Ask about mechanical training if the mine pays wages during it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years is enough for the mine to say which trucks it wants to automate. AGI would change planning by 2031 and capable robots could drive around 2034. If management knows its order book, it should share the dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when AGI arrives, I'd still be driving, but the office may set leaner rosters. I'd be 51 when the robots come. My older child will be nearly grown, but that doesn't tell me whether the mortgage is paid or whether anyone will hire a former driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor once a year what equipment is on order, and I'd keep my truck qualification current. If the first year after 2031 brings shorter rosters, I'd apply for paid yard driving at a nearby pit. Lena and I would use any steady overtime to reduce the mortgage balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, although I still don't fancy retraining for a job I don't understand. I can work with a date; I can't plan around a notice stuck on the gate on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI to read those equipment plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask the supervisor to explain them in plain words. A computer answer isn't much use if I can't tell whether it's right. I learn best by seeing the machine and asking the mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the yard job also becomes automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be looking again before 2034. I'm not calling yard driving a permanent answer; it would keep wages coming in while we decide what to do next.

say: I'd ask management for **equipment dates** rather than vague reassurance.
I'd explain that **planning** changes in 2031 and robot driving may follow around 2034.
think: At **51** the robot date could end my driving income before I know what work comes next.
An older child means different costs, not a paid **mortgage** or guaranteed job.
do: Ask the supervisor yearly about **truck orders** and keep my qualification current.
Apply for paid **yard driving** after 2031 if rosters shorten.
Use steady overtime to **reduce the mortgage** while it is available.
feel: Still **anxious**, but able to plan around dates.
S3.quote: I can work with a date; I can't plan around a notice stuck on the gate on Friday.
fieldNote: Femi remains attached to **familiar driving**, even as he acknowledges that another driving post may also be temporary.
His willingness to pay down the **mortgage** depends on steady overtime, which is never assumed.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor yearly about equipment orders and maintain truck qualification
Apply for paid yard driving after 2031 if rosters shorten
Use steady overtime to reduce the mortgage balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years should mean a published schedule for new equipment. AGI in 2036 may take planning and records; robots around 2039 could take the truck seats. Nobody should discover their last shift by reading a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 at the thinking-AI date and 56 when capable robots reach driving. The children will be grown then, but I can't assume the mortgage has vanished or a pension starts at 56. I want to stay employed, even if the job has to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and ask at each yearly review whether the mine will fund a paid equipment inspection course. If it did, I'd enroll and try the practical part with a mechanic; otherwise I'd keep my qualification and watch for paid vacancies. After 2036 I'd apply for inspection work if I had completed that course, before the truck seats change around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me room to ask questions without choking on them. I still don't love new software, but I could learn a hands-on inspection routine if someone showed me at the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on that inspection job lasting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Full AGI could help check records, and robots might eventually do the physical checks too. I'd take paid inspection work while it existed and keep the mortgage lower if we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the mine besides a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the terms on one sheet: hours, pay, who qualifies, and which jobs are real. I don't need a motivational talk; I need to know whether a course still lets me cover Thursday's mortgage debit.

say: I'd demand a published **equipment schedule** well before robot trucks arrive.
I'd say **AGI** changes records in 2036 and capable robots may reach driving around 2039.
think: At **56** I may still need wages and cannot assume a pension or a paid-off house.
I could learn inspection at a machine, but **AI records** and robots may eventually reach that job.
do: Keep driving and ask each year about a **paid inspection course**.
Enroll only if the mine funds training and keeps **wages** coming.
Apply for paid **inspection posts** after 2036 if I complete the course.
feel: **Cautiously steadier**, though still wary of software and lost work.
S4.quote: Nobody should discover their last shift by reading a roster.
fieldNote: A decade makes Femi more willing to discuss **practical training**, provided wages continue and the terms are explicit.
He expects to need **paid work** at 56 and does not treat inspection as permanent protection.

steps.text: Keep driving and ask yearly about paid inspection training
Enroll in equipment inspection training only if wages continue
Apply for paid inspection posts after 2036 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the three years to robot trucks leave me trying to find wages while the children still depend on us. A written equipment schedule would help, and so would training that pays wages throughout. I'd like someone to tell us what jobs exist, not just what skills sound good.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the people who are still learning the old job. I don't have years of seniority to trade on. If the mine offers a course, put the pay and shift times on the notice so a family can decide.

headlineQuote: I don't have years of seniority to trade on.
portrait: Femi is a **43-year-old junior miner** who drives a haul truck at a large mine.
He shares a **mortgage** and two school-age children's costs with Lena, with a few months of expenses saved.
He trusts paper fault notes and practical instruction, and has **never used AI tools**.
He fears rapid robot driving most; longer warning allows **conditional training** while he keeps paid work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Femi too little time before robot trucks could threaten his driving wages around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A written **equipment schedule** and training that keeps wages coming would let his family plan.
